KEY MESSAGE 1...
After a very pleasant Fall, the coldest air of the season is
finally set to invade the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, and
Northeast tonight through the weekend as a deep mid/upper 
trough digs into the eastern CONUS. Satellite and water vapor 
loops this afternoon show a highly amplified pattern developing 
as sharp mid/upper ridging strengthens over the western CONUS, 
with a downstream trough digging into the Upper Midwest. Clouds
have already thickened up across the region ahead of this
upstream trough and developing surface low, with regional radar
showing an expanding area of showers near Chicago. As the
mid/upper trough continues to dig into the Great Lakes and Ohio
Valley tonight, coupling between a 50-70 knot H5 jet rounding
its base toward the Tennessee Valley and a 50 knot H5 southern
stream jet offshore of the Carolinas will help the surface low
to rapidly deepen as it tracks across central/southern Ohio
tonight then offshore of southern New Jersey by Thursday 
evening.

An initial cold front will settle south across Lake Erie this
afternoon and through the rest of the region this evening, with
minimal impacts other than a wind shift to light northerly. The
main impact will come with the deepening surface low that tracks
just south of the CWA tonight and early Thursday morning.
Strengthening mid-level frontogenesis on the north and 
northwest side of the low track beneath upper divergence will
lead to continued expansion of the upstream rain, and a modest
850 jet response to the forcing could advect in enough mid-
level instability for some weak convective elements to support
briefly heavier rain. With this being said, expect scattered
light showers this evening to become a widespread, steadier
rain after 04Z, with rain then lasting much of the night and
tapering off from west to east in the 12-15Z Thursday timeframe.
The steadiest rain and biggest risk area for some heavier 
convective downpours will be from north central Ohio through NE 
Ohio and NW PA in closer proximity to the strengthening 
dynamics. Overall, this system will be a soaker, but rainfall 
amounts will remain very manageable in the 0.25 to 0.60 inch 
range given the fast movement. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
The real change to much colder air will come in the wake of the
low Thursday as the center of the mid/upper trough settles over
the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes bringing a pool of 0 to -3 C
850 mb air overhead. This will set up a raw, damp day as the
tightening pressure gradient and cold air advection lead to N
winds gusting up to 30 mph at times and highs only in the upper
40s falling a bit further in the afternoon. There will be a 
lull in the rain Thursday morning in most areas, but expect 
widespread showers to rotate back into the region for the 
afternoon and evening ahead of a mid- level shortwave and 
associated surface trough dropping southward coupled with deep 
wraparound moisture and growing lake to 850 mb delta T's. This 
will set up round two of fairly steady rain, with maximum 
coverage in the 18-00Z timeframe. The greatest amounts will 
occur over the central highlands as well as inland portions of 
the primary and secondary snowbelts of NE Ohio and NW PA where 
lake enhancement and upslope flow will boost totals. These areas
could see an additional 0.25 to 0.50 inch of rain.

By Thursday night, even colder air in the wake of the
shortwave/surface trough and continued northerly flow will
transition the precip to pure lake effect, which will continue
at varying coverages and intensities through Saturday as weak
shortwave impulses rotate through. An average boundary layer
flow near 360 degrees coupled with sufficient wraparound
moisture and strong lake induced instability will set up a Lake
Huron band from the Lake Erie Islands to the central highlands
Thursday night and Friday morning, with scattered, lighter
showers across NE Ohio and NW PA given the short fetch. Locally
heavy downpours will accompany this band, with graupel within 
the strongest convective cores. The warm lake and strong 
northerly flow will advect the marine layer inland, so expect 
temperatures to be too warm in most areas for snow flakes 
Thursday night/Friday morning, however, the higher elevations of
the central highlands as well as interior NE Ohio and NW PA 
will likely see some wet snow. Accumulations likely won't amount
to more than a slushy dusting, but will need to watch for wet 
bulbing in the stronger Huron band that could lead to locally 
more snow (1-2 inches at most). 

Precip should transition back to mainly rain during the day
Friday, and expect the main Huron band to slowly pivot eastward
into NE Ohio and NW PA as the boundary layer flow backs to NW.
This will lead to a more traditional, multi-band lake effect set
up Friday evening through Saturday over the primary and
secondary snowbelts. Graupel and wet snow will be possible
during the day Friday in the heaviest convective bursts, mainly
in the highest elevations,
